title: Herringbone stitch
subtitle: Crossed diagonal stitches that build a woven band or border
excerpt: Herringbone stitch crosses diagonal stitches in alternate directions to form a woven pattern that works as a border, band fill, or decorative grid.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), herringbone entry.
heroPrompt: Herringbone stitch border in red cotton thread on cream linen, the regular X pattern forming a neat diagonal band, close-up, natural light.

content.text: Herringbone works between two parallel guide lines. Each stitch travels diagonally to one line, makes a small backward step along it, then crosses diagonally to the other line and steps back there. The alternating direction of travel creates the X crossings that give the stitch its woven look.
Draw two parallel lines about 8 mm apart. Bring the needle up at the bottom-left.
Insert at the top line, 8 mm to the right. Bring up 3 mm to the left on the top line.
Insert at the bottom line, 8 mm to the right of where you started. Bring up 3 mm to the left on the bottom line.
Continue in this zigzag rhythm. Each stitch crosses the previous one at the guide lines.

items.cause: The backward step on each line is not consistent.
items.fix: Keep the backward step the same length every time: 2 to 3 mm.

items.symptom: The angles are too shallow and the pattern looks flat
items.cause: Guide lines are too close together or spacing between stitches is too wide.
items.fix: Use two parallel lines at least 8 mm apart and keep forward spacing at 6 to 8 mm.

content.text: Herringbone stitch forms the base for interlaced herringbone, where a second thread is woven through the crossings without entering the fabric. Closed herringbone (with no step) is a seam stitch and the basis of shadow work.
